content: Aortitis, Infectious 1. The preferred treatment regimen for infectious aortitis includes cefotaxime sodium at a dose of 1–2 g administered intravenously once daily. 2. Alternatively, ciprofloxacin hydrochloride can be used at a dose of 400 mg intravenously every 12 hours, or 500–750 mg orally every 12 hours. Levofloxacin is another option, dosed at 250–750 mg intravenously or orally once daily. 3. Another regimen involves oxacillin or nafcillin at 1–2 g administered intravenously or intramuscularly every 4–6 hours. Dicloxacillin at 500 mg to 1 g intravenously or intramuscularly every 4–6 hours is also an option. 4. Vancomycin can be used at a dose of 1 g (15 mg/kg, up to 30–40 g/day) intravenously every 12 hours. 5. It is critical to initiate broad-spectrum, bactericidal antibiotics after obtaining blood cultures and before surgery. For patients with a creatinine clearance (CCr) ≤ 20 mL/min, the cefotaxime dose should be reduced by 50%. Ciprofloxacin should be used cautiously in patients with a CCr ≤ 50 mL/min or when co-administered with drugs that may alter its metabolism. Cardiovascular Implantable Electronic Device (CIED) Infections 1. Early Post-Implantation Inflammation: The preferred treatment is flucloxacillin at 0.5–1 g orally three times daily. 2. Penicillin Allergy or MRSA Colonization: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, linezolid 600 mg orally twice daily, or clindamycin 450 mg orally four times daily are recommended. 3. Uncomplicated Generator Pocket Infection: Vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours, daptomycin 4 mg/kg intravenously once daily, or teicoplanin 6 mg/kg (up to 1 g) intravenously at 0, 12, and 24 hours, then daily, are preferred. 4. Complicated Generator Pocket Infection with Pending Blood Cultures: Vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours combined with meropenem 1 g intravenously every 8 hours, or daptomycin 8–10 mg/kg intravenously once daily combined with meropenem 1 g intravenously every 8 hours, is recommended. 5. Generator Pocket Infection with Negative Blood Cultures: Vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours combined with gentamicin 1 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours, or daptomycin 8–10 mg/kg intravenously once daily combined with gentamicin 1 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours, is preferred. 6. For complicated infections, such as endocarditis, septic thrombophlebitis, or osteomyelitis, antimicrobial therapy should last at least 4–6 weeks. Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections 1. Staphylococcus aureus (Methicillin-Susceptible): Nafcillin or oxacillin at 2 g intravenously every 6 hours is preferred. Alternatives include cefazolin 2 g intravenously every 8 hours or vancomycin 15 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours. 2. Staphylococcus aureus (Methicillin-Resistant): Vancomycin 15 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours, daptomycin 6–8 mg/kg per day intravenously, or linezolid intravenously are recommended. Rifampin or gentamicin may be added if susceptibility is confirmed. 3. Coagulase-Negative Staphylococci (Methicillin-Susceptible): Nafcillin or oxacillin 2 g intravenously every 4 hours is preferred. Alternatives include first-generation cephalosporins, vancomycin, or TMP-SMZ. 4. Coagulase-Negative Staphylococci (Methicillin-Resistant): Vancomycin 15 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours is preferred. Alternatives include daptomycin 6 mg/kg per day intravenously or linezolid intravenously. 5. Enterococcus faecalis/faecium (Ampicillin-Susceptible): Ampicillin 2 g intravenously every 4–6 hours or gentamicin 1 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours is preferred. Vancomycin is an alternative. 6. Enterococcus faecalis/faecium (Ampicillin-Resistant, Vancomycin-Susceptible): Vancomycin 15 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours, with or without gentamicin, is preferred. Alternatives include linezolid or daptomycin. 7. Enterococcus faecalis/faecium (Ampicillin-Resistant, Vancomycin-Resistant): Linezolid 600 mg intravenously every 12 hours or daptomycin 6 mg/kg per day intravenously is preferred. Quinupristin/dalfopristin is an alternative. Mediastinitis, Acute 1. For mediastinitis secondary to cardiac infection or surgery, the preferred treatment is clindamycin 450 mg intravenously every 6 hours combined with ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily for at least 2 weeks. 2. Prophylaxis for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus involves second-generation cephalosporins, while methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus requires vancomycin. 3. Aggressive surgical debridement is essential for deep sternal wound infections. 4. Maintaining postoperative blood glucose levels ≤180 mg/dL with continuous intravenous insulin protocols is advised to reduce infection risk. Myocarditis, Viral 1. Supportive care and standard management of congestive heart failure (CHF) are the mainstays of therapy for viral myocarditis. Ribavirin and interferon-alpha have shown improved survival in animal models. 2. Temporary pacemaker insertion is indicated for symptomatic bradycardia or heart block during the acute phase. 3. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) are not recommended during the acute phase but may be beneficial for life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias in the chronic phase. 4. Antiarrhythmic therapy is useful for symptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT) or sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) during the acute phase. Pericarditis, Tuberculous 1. The preferred regimen includes isoniazid 5 mg/kg (300 mg) once daily, rifampicin 10 mg/kg (600 mg) once daily, pyrazinamide 1,500 mg once daily, and ethambutol 1,200 mg once daily for 2 months, followed by rifampicin and pyrazinamide for 4 months. 2. Prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg per day is given for 5–7 days and tapered over 6–8 weeks. Rheumatic Fever, Primary Prophylaxis 1. Penicillin V 500 mg orally 2–3 times daily for 10 days, amoxicillin 50 mg/kg orally once daily (maximum 1 g) for 10 days, or benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly (600,000 U for patients ≤27 kg; 1,200,000 U for patients >27 kg) once are preferred regimens. 2. Alternatives include narrow-spectrum cephalosporins, clindamycin, azithromycin, or clarithromycin. Septic Pelvic Vein Thrombophlebitis 1. For right ovarian vein thrombosis, the preferred regimen is ertapenem 1 g orally once daily for 7 days combined with enoxaparin initially, followed by 3–6 months of warfarin (INR 2.5). 2. For pelvic branch vein thrombosis, ertapenem 1 g orally once daily for 7 days combined with enoxaparin for 2 weeks is recommended.
